what: Piper Sandler is a US investment bank focused on mid-sized companies, advising on mergers and acquisitions, raising equity and debt capital, underwriting municipal bonds and trading for institutional investors.
customers: Mid-sized companies, private equity firms, municipalities and institutional investors.
money: Fees from advising on mergers, acquisitions and restructurings
Underwriting stock and debt offerings, including for healthcare and financial companies
Municipal bond underwriting plus equity and fixed income trading for institutions
moat: A strong brand in middle-market M&A and in sectors such as healthcare, financial services and public finance, built on senior bankers and relationships.
risks: Advisory fees fall quickly when deal activity slows
Pay is the main cost and senior bankers can leave
Capital markets revenue depends on open IPO and bond markets
opportunities: Revenue recovered from $1.35 billion in 2023 to $2.08 billion over the last twelve months as deals returned
No reported debt and free cash flow of about $790 million over the last twelve months
Shareholders get a regular dividend plus special dividends and buybacks
watch: Announced M&A volumes in the middle market and the pace of new stock offerings.
view: Piper Sandler is a good example of how cyclical an investment bank is. Revenue fell from $2.03 billion in 2021 to $1.35 billion in 2023 when deal-making dried up, then climbed back to $2.08 billion over the last twelve months. Net income followed: $85 million in 2023 versus $302 million now.

At around 15 times trailing earnings and 13 times next year’s estimate, the shares are not expensive for a business with no reported debt and strong cash generation. The company returns much of that cash: dividends and buybacks together were about $240 million in 2025.

The risk is the cycle itself. When interest rates rise or markets wobble, companies postpone deals and advisory fees can drop by a third in a year, as 2022 showed. Anyone owning this stock is essentially taking a view on middle-market deal activity over the next few years.
bull: M&A and equity issuance keep recovering, margins expand on a fixed cost base and earnings grow about 18% next year as analysts expect.
bear: A slowdown in deal-making cuts advisory fees and margins fall back toward 2023 levels.
